question_bank.question: A team cannot find a public dataset for people saying the exact phrase “Robert, turn on.” What first data-collection move best matches the lecture's guidance?
choices: Ask willing people for permission, record their voices clearly, and use those real examples first.
Generate many synthetic voices first, then check later whether any real recordings are needed.
Record people nearby without interrupting them, then anonymize the files after training.
Reuse a generic wake-word dataset first, then assume the phrase mismatch is a small issue.
question_bank.explanation: The instructor highlights consent and real recordings as the practical early move: ask clearly, get freely given permission, and collect phrase-specific natural data.

source_ref.evidence_span: Get the permission to record and use their voice.

frame_evidence.description: Instructor stands by the whiteboard timeline while discussing asking people around campus to record the trigger phrase.

question_bank.question: Why does the lecture treat text-to-speech as useful but not the preferred first move for the wake-word dataset?
choices: It usually removes the need for negative examples, but it makes labeling harder to audit.
It guarantees realistic voices, but it usually takes longer to run than human recording.
It adds extra design choices such as voice diversity, which can slow early progress.
It makes the trigger phrase too short, which prevents sliding-window training.
question_bank.explanation: Synthetic speech can help, but it creates additional knobs: how many voices, how much diversity, and whether the generated distribution resembles real users.

source_ref.evidence_span: how many voices, how many different voices does it

frame_evidence.description: Whiteboard still shows the project sketch as the instructor contrasts real recordings with synthetic text-to-speech voices.

question_bank.question: What is the main advantage of gathering natural wake-word recordings early in this project?
choices: It makes the model architecture smaller before any training data is reviewed.
It turns every recording into a positive example, so negative sampling becomes unnecessary.
It removes the need to check whether people consented to data use.
It reduces uncertainty because the samples better match how users will actually speak.
question_bank.explanation: Natural recordings are valuable because they come from the target behavior itself, whereas synthetic data can look plausible yet miss model-relevant variation.

frame_evidence.description: Instructor gestures toward the board while explaining why synthetic audio can differ from true natural user speech.

question_bank.question: What makes the wake-word data bottleneck different from reusing a large generic speech dataset?
choices: The phrase-specific examples already exist online, but the labels are mostly noisy.
The exact custom phrase has no matching internet-scale dataset, so the team must collect it.
The public dataset has the right phrase, but it lacks enough background-noise clips.
The generic dataset has enough positives, but it cannot be used with neural networks.
question_bank.explanation: The instructor says there is no large internet dataset for the custom phrase, so the team has to build a matching dataset rather than rely on generic speech data.

source_ref.evidence_span: And it turns out that there is no data set on the internet

frame_evidence.description: Instructor points back to the wake-word setup on the whiteboard while explaining that the exact phrase dataset does not already exist.
